nodes.title: Electric Charge, Valence & Coulomb Forces
nodes.source_material: Khan Academy AP Physics 2: Electric Charge, Field, and Potential; Lecture 1a Slides 7-16
nodes.summary: Atomic origin of charge (protons, electrons, valence ions Na+, K+, Cl-, Proteins P-), charge conservation, macroscopic charge neutrality in ICF/ECF, and electrostatic attraction/repulsion via F = qE.
nodes.DiagnosticQuestion: Why does separating a tiny fraction of Na+ and Cl- across a 7.5 nm membrane create a strong electric field while the bulk ICF and ECF remain nearly charge neutral?

nodes.title: Electric Potential, Work & Relative Voltage
nodes.source_material: Khan Academy AP Physics 2: Electric Potential Energy & Voltage; Lecture 1a Slides 15-18; EN01 Lecture 1 Slides 4-11
nodes.summary: Definition of voltage as potential energy difference per unit charge (1 V = 1 J/C), why voltage is always relative to a reference (ECF ground = 0 V), and how ion pumps perform work against an electric field.
nodes.DiagnosticQuestion: If V_mem = -70 mV with ECF defined as ground (0 V), how much electrostatic work is required to move one mole of Na+ (z = +1) from ICF to ECF?

nodes.title: Electric Current & Membrane Capacitance
nodes.source_material: Khan Academy AP Physics 2 & EE Intro: Current & Capacitors; Backgrounders Quiz Q1b; Sam & Max Problems Slides 14-19
nodes.summary: Current as rate of charge flow (I = dQ/dt), conventional current direction for positive vs. negative ions, and parallel-plate capacitor relations (Q = C*V) for the lipid bilayer membrane.
equations: I = dQ / dt = z * F * J_ion * A_cell
nodes.DiagnosticQuestion: Backgrounders Quiz: How much charge (in Coulombs) is stored on a 50 nF capacitor at 100 mV? How does adding a thick myelin sheath (series capacitance) change total membrane capacitance?

nodes.title: Ohm's Law, Conductance & Circuit Elements
nodes.source_material: Khan Academy EE: Circuit Analysis; Circuits Backgrounder Slides 2-3, 7-8, 12; Backgrounders Quiz Q1a
nodes.summary: Ideal voltage sources (batteries), ideal current sources (ion pumps), linear resistors (ion channels), Ohm's Law (V = IR), and reciprocal conductance (G = 1/R, I = GV).
nodes.DiagnosticQuestion: Backgrounders Quiz: How much current flows through a 20 Ohm resistor with 100 mV across it, in amps and in mA?

nodes.title: KVL, KCL, Series/Parallel & Voltage/Current Dividers
nodes.source_material: Khan Academy AP Physics 2 & EE: Kirchhoff's Laws; Circuits Backgrounder Slides 4-11; Sam & Max Problems Slides 4-13
nodes.summary: Kirchhoff's Voltage Law (sum of potential drops around any closed loop is zero), Kirchhoff's Current Law (sum of currents entering a node is zero), series/parallel resistor combinations, and voltage/current dividers.
nodes.DiagnosticQuestion: In a two-resistor voltage divider between V_1 = +80 mV (R_1 = 40 Ohm) and V_2 = -80 mV (R_2 = 10 Ohm), why does the middle node voltage settle much closer to -80 mV?

nodes.title: Nodal Analysis of Multi-Branch Cell Circuits
nodes.source_material: Khan Academy EE: Nodal Analysis; Circuits Backgrounder Slides 14-17; Backgrounders Quiz Part 2 Q1-Q2
nodes.summary: Applying KCL at the intracellular fluid (ICF) node with parallel Nernst batteries (V_N,Na, V_N,K, V_N,Cl), channel conductances (G_Na, G_K, G_Cl), and Na+/K+ pump current sources to solve for V_mem analytically and intuitively.
equations: G_Na*(V_mem - V_N,Na) + G_K*(V_mem - V_N,K) + G_Cl*(V_mem - V_N,Cl) + I_pump,Na + I_pump,K = 0
V_mem = (G_Na*V_N,Na + G_K*V_N,K + G_Cl*V_N,Cl - I_pump,net) / (G_Na + G_K + G_Cl)
nodes.DiagnosticQuestion: Backgrounders Quiz Part 2: Given V_N,Na=77mV (G=0.4), V_N,K=-89mV (G=2.2), V_N,Cl=-71mV (G=0.4), I_Na=60, I_K=-40, compute V_ICF. What happens if G_K becomes 100x larger?

nodes.title: Thevenin/Norton Equivalents & RC Delay Dynamics
nodes.source_material: Khan Academy EE: Thevenin's Theorem & RC Circuits; Circuits Backgrounder Slides 18-25
nodes.summary: Collapsing a multi-channel single-cell circuit into a single Thevenin voltage (V_th) and resistance (R_th) to analyze multicellular gap-junction networks and RC membrane charging time constants (tau = R_th * C_mem).
nodes.DiagnosticQuestion: How does replacing each cell's 5-branch circuit with its Thevenin equivalent simplify solving for V_mem across two cells coupled by a gap-junction resistor R_GJ?

nodes.title: Exponential Relaxation ODEs & 2D Vector Projections
nodes.source_material: Tufts MATH 32 Prereq; Lab 4 (Neuron HH ODEs); Lecture 3 Slide 25 (Vector Math Review)
nodes.summary: First-order linear ODEs for channel gating relaxation dx/dt = (x_inf - x)/tau, Hill function non-linearities, and 2D vector addition / dot-product projections for cardiac dipole leads.
nodes.DiagnosticQuestion: If m(0) = 0.4 and m_inf suddenly jumps to 0.9 with tau_m = 10 ms, write the trajectory m(t) and compare its initial slope to tau_m = 20 ms.

nodes.title: Python, NumPy Vectorization & BITSEY Architecture
nodes.source_material: EN 01 Python Lectures; EE 123 sim.py, sim_toolbox.py, edebug.py, eplot.py
nodes.summary: Using Python, Thonny, and NumPy 2D arrays cc_cells[n_ions, n_cells] and Dm_array[n_ions, n_cells] to simulate ion fluxes, adaptive explicit vs. BDF implicit ODE integration, and Gate objects in BITSEY.
equations: V_mem = F * sum_i(z_i * cc_cells[i]) * V_cell / (A_cell * C_m)
nodes.DiagnosticQuestion: In BITSEY's sim.py, why are all ion fluxes (pumps, channels, and gap junctions) normalized per m^2 of total cell membrane area before multiplying by cell_sa / cell_vol?

nodes.title: Central Dogma, Transcription Factors & Gene Logic
nodes.source_material: EE 123 Lecture 4a: Biology Backgrounder (4a_bio_backgrounder.pptx Slides 1-25)
nodes.summary: The cell as a hardware/software machine: DNA bases/codons as software, transcription (DNA -> mRNA) and translation (mRNA -> tRNA/ribosome -> folded proteins), promoters as conditional if-then statements, and transcription factors (TFs) forming gene regulatory networks (GRNs).
equations: DNA (4^3 = 64 codons) -> mRNA -> Protein (20 amino acids)
nodes.DiagnosticQuestion: If every cell in your body has the exact same DNA software, how do promoters and transcription factors allow a toe cell and an eye cell to express completely different proteins?

nodes.title: Fick's Law of Diffusion & Skittles Lab
nodes.source_material: EE 123 Lecture 1a Slides 21-28; Lecture 2a Slide 6; Real Lab 1: Skittles Diffusion (lab_skittles.pdf)
nodes.summary: Thermal random walk of particles, Fick's First Law (j_diff = -D dC/dx), why diffusion time scales quadratically with distance (t ~ L^2 / D), and why macroscopic organisms cannot rely on pure diffusion for long-range signaling.
nodes.DiagnosticQuestion: Lab 1 Question: Why does diffusing over twice the distance take 4x as much time, and why do colored zones in the Skittles experiment form sharp boundaries initially?

nodes.title: Ion Drift Flux, Mobility & Membrane Ohm's Law
nodes.source_material: EE 123 Lecture 1a Slides 29-40
nodes.summary: Electrostatic drift of ions in a membrane electric field (E = V_mem/L), terminal drift velocity from viscous drag (v = mu * f = mu * z * q * V_mem / L), Einstein relation (mu = D / k_B T), and microscopic derivation of Ohm's Law.
equations: j_drift = -C_ion * v_drift = -C_ion * mu_ion * z * q * (V_mem / L)
nodes.DiagnosticQuestion: Why does a constant electric field produce a constant ion drift velocity rather than constant acceleration across the ion channel?

nodes.title: Semi-Permeable Membranes & The Nernst Equation
nodes.source_material: EE 123 Lecture 1a Slides 41-59
nodes.summary: Equilibrium potential where inward/outward diffusion flux exactly balances electrostatic drift flux (j_diff + j_drift = 0), deriving the Nernst potential V_Nernst, and computing V_N for Na+ (+57 mV), K+ (-78 mV), and Cl- (-62 mV) in giant squid axons.
equations: V_Nernst = (R * T) / (z * F) * ln([ion]_ECF / [ion]_ICF) approx (26 mV / z) * ln([ion]_ECF / [ion]_ICF)
nodes.DiagnosticQuestion: In a cell resting at V_mem = -60 mV, why does Cl- satisfy the Nernst equation (drift balances diffusion), whereas Na+ has both drift and diffusion pointing inward?

nodes.title: Na+/K+-ATPase Pumps, Detailed Balance vs. Steady State
nodes.source_material: EE 123 Lecture 1a Slides 60-81; sim_toolbox.py (GHK & pumpNaKATP)
nodes.summary: Active transport via the Na+/K+-ATPase pump (3 Na+ out, 2 K+ in per ATP hydrolyzed), distinguishing thermodynamic equilibrium (detailed balance, Cl-) from energy-consuming Steady State (SS, where j_channel + j_pump = 0 for each ion individually), and the linear vs. GHK flux models.
equations: j_total,i = G_i * (V_mem - V_N,i) + j_pump,i = 0 (for each ion i in SS)
nodes.DiagnosticQuestion: Explain the difference between equilibrium (detailed balance) and steady state in a living cell: which ions are in equilibrium and which are only in steady state?

nodes.title: Sim Lab 2: Steady-State Bioelectricity in BITSEY
nodes.source_material: EE 123 Sim Lab 2 (slab_simple_SS.pdf, main_sim_SS.py)
nodes.summary: Simulating 4 cells over 100,000 seconds in BITSEY (SS1 baseline, SS2 doubled initial [Na]/[K]/[Cl] with electroneutrality, SS3 doubled D_Na/D_K/D_Cl) to prove that steady-state V_mem and concentrations are determined by channel conductances and robust to initial concentration perturbations.
equations: 4 equations (Q=CV, J_Na=0, J_K=0, J_Cl=0) in 4 unknowns ([Na]_ICF, [K]_ICF, [Cl]_ICF, V_mem)
Doubling D_Cl leaves SS V_mem unchanged; doubling D_Na depolarizes; doubling D_K hyperpolarizes
nodes.DiagnosticQuestion: Why does doubling D_Cl in cell #3 have zero effect on the final steady-state V_mem, whereas doubling initial [Na]_ICF in SS2 eventually returns to the exact same state as cell #0?

nodes.title: Quasi-Steady State (QSS) & Fast Capacitive Settling
nodes.source_material: EE 123 Lecture 1b (1b_bioelec_QSS.pptx Slides 1-36); Sim Lab 3 (slab_simple_QSS.pdf, main_sim_QSS.py); Oral Quiz #1
nodes.summary: Two-timescale dynamics of V_mem: why changing G_Na or G_K slews V_mem in milliseconds (QSS) while bulk ion concentrations take hours to change (SS). In QSS, net charge flux sum(z_i * j_i) = 0 even though individual ion fluxes are non-zero.
equations: dV_mem / dt = I_net / C_mem = (F * Vol / (A * c_m)) * sum_i(z_i * slew_cc_i)
QSS condition: I_Na + I_K + I_Cl + I_pump,net = 0 (net charge flux = 0, individual j_i != 0)
nodes.DiagnosticQuestion: Oral Quiz #1 & Sim Lab 3: Does KCL on the cell equivalent circuit compute the QSS V_mem or the SS V_mem? Why does changing V_mem by 100 mV require moving only a negligible fraction of intracellular Na+ ions?

nodes.title: Hodgkin-Huxley Action Potentials & Gating ODEs
nodes.source_material: EE 123 Lecture 2a Slides 8-14; Sim Lab 4: Building a Neuron (slab_neurons.pdf, main_sim_neuron.py)
nodes.summary: Voltage-gated Na+ and K+ channels in the Hodgkin-Huxley model: fast positive feedback via m^3 (tau_m small, m_inf increasing) launches the depolarization spike toward V_N,Na; slower negative feedback via Na+ inactivation h (h_inf decreasing, tau_h > tau_m) and K+ activation n^4 (n_inf increasing, tau_n approx tau_h) terminates the spike and creates the refractory period.
equations: g_Na(V,t) = g_Na_max * m^3 * h,   g_K(V,t) = g_K_max * n^4
dm/dt = (m_inf(V) - m)/tau_m,  dh/dt = (h_inf(V) - h)/tau_h,  dn/dt = (n_inf(V) - n)/tau_n
nodes.DiagnosticQuestion: Sim Lab 4: How do increasing tau_h and tau_n vs. increasing tau_m affect action potential peak voltage and spike width, and how do m^3*h and n^4 explain the refractory period?

nodes.title: Axonal Propagation, Myelin Capacitance & Synapses
nodes.source_material: EE 123 Lecture 2a Slides 15-31
nodes.summary: Spatial propagation of action potentials via local axial diffusion/drift, why the refractory period prevents backward reflection, how myelin sheaths reduce membrane capacitance (Q=CV) for rapid saltatory conduction between Nodes of Ranvier, and chemical synaptic transmission (neurotransmitters, CNS vs. PNS, afferent vs. efferent, reflex arcs & CPGs).
equations: C_myelinated << C_bare  =>  smaller Delta_Q needed for Delta_V  =>  v_prop up to 150 m/s
V_dendrite = sum_k w_k * V_syn,k >= V_threshold => AP trigger
nodes.DiagnosticQuestion: Why does wrapping an axon in myelin decrease its capacitance, why does lower capacitance speed up propagation, and why are bare Nodes of Ranvier still required periodically?

nodes.title: Motor Units, sEMG, Nerve Conduction (NCS) & DSP Filtering
nodes.source_material: EE 123 Lecture 2b Slides 10-29; Real Lab 5: sEMG (lab_semg.pdf); EN01 Lectures 3, 4 & Lab 4 (Moving Avg, RMS, Frequency Domain)
nodes.summary: Sensory encoding (one-hot olfaction vs. encoded trichromatic vision, thermal grill illusion), motor unit recruitment (Henneman size principle, rate coding, spatial interlacing), Compound Muscle Action Potential (CMAP), skin as a low-pass filter, diagnostic Nerve Conduction Studies (diabetic neuropathy vs. MS demyelination vs. sciatica), and sEMG signal processing (60 Hz noise, moving-average baseline removal, segment RMS).
equations: sEMG usable bandwidth: 10-500 Hz (peak energy 50-150 Hz); power-line noise = 60 Hz
nodes.DiagnosticQuestion: Lab 5 & Lecture 2b: How does spatial interlacing of motor units allow a surface electrode to measure a smooth RMS force ramp, and how does an NCS distinguish diabetic axonal loss from MS demyelination?

nodes.title: Myoelectric Prosthetics, TMR & AMI Interfaces
nodes.source_material: EE 123 Lecture 2b Slides 30-44; Lab 5 Discussion Q3
nodes.summary: Controlling multi-DoF prosthetic limbs using differential biceps/triceps sEMG signals, co-contraction mode switching, Targeted Muscle Reinnervation (TMR) for routing amputated residual nerves to denervated muscle patches, and Agonist-Antagonist Myoneural Interfaces (AMI) to restore proprioceptive feedback and reduce phantom limb pain.
equations: Mode switch trigger: (RMS_biceps > Theta) AND (RMS_triceps > Theta)
nodes.DiagnosticQuestion: For a trans-radial vs. trans-humeral amputee, what are the pros and cons of biceps/triceps sEMG control, and why must TMR denervate part of the target muscle first?

nodes.title: Gate-Control Theory of Pain, SCS, PNS & Electroceuticals
nodes.source_material: EE 123 Lecture 2b Slides 45-82; Oral Quiz #2
nodes.summary: Nociception vs. pain perception, Melzack-Wall Gate-Control Theory (A-delta/C pain fibers vs. A-beta touch fibers driving an inhibitory interneuron), conventional paresthesia Spinal Cord Stimulation (35-80 Hz) vs. paresthesia-free 10 kHz / 500 Hz burst SCS, Peripheral Nerve Stimulation (PNS), vagus nerve anti-inflammatory electroceuticals (SetPoint, Saluda closed-loop ECAP, Neuspera, Cala Health), and Wolff's Law piezoelectric bone growth (SparkSpine).
equations: Pain_out = max(0, w_nociceptor * I_Adelta_C - w_inhib * (I_Abeta - w_inh_block * I_Adelta_C))
Conventional SCS: 35-80 Hz, 210-450 us, 4-8 mA; HF SCS: 10 kHz paresthesia-free
nodes.DiagnosticQuestion: Oral Quiz #2: Explain the Gate-Control Theory circuit (how rubbing a pinched finger relieves pain), and discuss which clinical observations of 10 kHz SCS challenge classical gate theory.

nodes.title: Cardiac Conduction System, Funny Channels & Gap Junctions
nodes.source_material: EE 123 Lecture 3 (3_GJs_cardiac.pptx Slides 1-22)
nodes.summary: Heart plumbing vs. electrical system (heart attack vs. cardiac arrest), pathway from Sinoatrial (SA) node -> atria (1 m/s) -> slow Atrioventricular (AV) node delay -> Bundle of His -> Bundle Branches -> fast Purkinje fibers, pacemaker automaticity via HCN 'funny' channels, and intercellular Gap Junctions (GJs) synchronizing 500,000 SA node cells via mutual entrainment.
equations: f_GJ = GJ_Ith(diffusion) + GJ_Gth * Delta_V_GJ(drift)  (Norton GJ model in BITSEY)
nodes.DiagnosticQuestion: How do gap junctions allow 500,000 noisy, independent SA-node pacemaker cells to entrain to a single unified heartbeat frequency, and why is AV-node conduction purposefully slow?

nodes.title: ECG Physics, Dipole Vector Projections & 6/12-Lead Geometry
nodes.source_material: EE 123 Lecture 3 Slides 23-42; Real Lab 6: Electrocardiogram (lab_ecg.pdf, 6lead_plot.py)
nodes.summary: Modeling the depolarizing myocardium as a moving current dipole vector, dot-product projection onto Einthoven limb leads (I = LA-RA at 0 deg, II = LL-RA at +60 deg, III = LL-LA at +120 deg) and Wilson's Central Terminal augmented leads (aVL, aVR, aVF), P-Q-R-S-T wave origins, computing the electrical R-axis angle, Right-Leg Drive (RLD) common-mode noise cancellation, and why biceps clenching corrupts specific ECG leads.
equations: Lead I = V_LA - V_RA (0 deg), Lead II = V_LL - V_RA (+60 deg), Lead III = V_LL - V_LA (+120 deg)
aVF = 1.5*(V_LL - W) (+90 deg), aVL = 1.5*(V_LA - W) (-30 deg), aVR = 1.5*(V_RA - W) (-150 deg)
nodes.DiagnosticQuestion: Lab 6: Why does clenching your left biceps introduce EMG noise only into Lead I, whereas clenching your right biceps corrupts both Lead I and Lead II? Why is there almost zero voltage drop between your left shoulder and left wrist ('CardioMan' resistor grid)?

nodes.title: Cardiac Arrhythmias, Triple-Redundancy Fail-Safes & Pacemakers
nodes.source_material: EE 123 Lecture 3 Slides 43-82; Oral Quiz #3
nodes.summary: AV blocks, Atrial Fibrillation (ectopic triggers, unidirectional block, reentrant loops at ~300 bpm, missing P waves, irregular QRS, pulmonary vein ablation / electroporation), Premature Ventricular Contractions (PVCs & endurance athlete bradycardia), biological triple-redundancy overdrive suppression (SA ~60 bpm > AV ~40 bpm > Purkinje ~20 bpm), electronic pacemakers, and autonomic baroreflex neuromodulation (Barostim).
equations: f_SA (~60 bpm) > f_AV (~40 bpm) > f_Purkinje (~20 bpm)  (Overdrive suppression hierarchy)
Reentrant loop condition: L_path / v_conduction > T_refractory
nodes.DiagnosticQuestion: Oral Quiz #3: How does having progressively slower downstream oscillators (SA 60 bpm, AV 40 bpm, Purkinje 20 bpm) guarantee that backup pacemakers stay silent during normal operation but take over on upstream failure? Why are endurance athletes more prone to PVCs and AFib?

nodes.title: Morphogenesis as a Layered Bioelectric System
nodes.source_material: EE 123 Lecture 4b: Weird Nature and Morphogenesis (4b_morphogenesis.pptx Slides 1-53)
nodes.summary: Open-loop DNA growth rules vs. closed-loop goal-directed anatomical homeostasis: scrambled 'Picasso' tadpole craniofacial remodeling, ectopic eye/brain induction via V_mem manipulation (Notch ICD, Kir6.1), planarian regeneration across 279 fragments, trophic memory in deer antlers and fiddler crabs, 1-octanol GJ blockade producing 2-headed or multi-species flatworm heads, and the two-layer architecture (Layer 1 builds V_mem pattern API -> Layer 2 executes GRN differentiation).
equations: Layer 1: Bioelectric Network (ICs + GJs + Morphogens) -> Spatial V_mem(x) Pattern API
Layer 2: V_mem(x) -> Transcription Factor / GRN -> Anatomical Organ Specification
nodes.DiagnosticQuestion: What experimental evidence in Xenopus tadpoles and planaria demonstrates that a spatial V_mem pattern acts as a high-level 'API' instructing downstream gene expression where to build an eye or a head?

nodes.title: Planarian Polarity Modeling: Electrodiffusion, Hill Feedback & GJ Scaling
nodes.source_material: EE 123 Lecture 4c: Worms (4c_worm.pptx Slides 1-55); Grodstein & Levin (2021, 2022)
nodes.summary: Engineering a regenerating 5-cell planarian in BITSEY: why a simple GJ resistor chain fails upon amputation, introducing a negatively charged morphogen M that redistributes via Nernst drift-diffusion across the worm, closing the positive-feedback loop in every cell via a steep Hill inverter on K+ channels ([M] high -> G_K low -> V_mem high -> attracts more M), morphogen generation/decay scaling, and GJ conductance regimes (R_GJ -> inf 'archipelago', optimal gradient, 2-headed regeneration, and R_GJ -> 0 short-circuit collapse).
equations: G_K(cell) = G_K,max / (1 + ([M]_cell / K_M)^N)  (Hill inverter positive feedback)
nodes.DiagnosticQuestion: In the 5-cell BITSEY planarian model, why does positive feedback between [M] and G_K in every cell allow an excised middle trunk fragment to regenerate its head-tail V_mem gradient, and what happens when R_GJ is too large vs. too small?

nodes.title: Bioelectric Oncology: Depolarization, GJ Isolation & Atavism
nodes.source_material: EE 123 Lecture 4c: Cancer (4c_cancer.pptx Slides 1-18); Final Projects Doc
nodes.summary: Classical somatic mutation theory (mitosis, differentiation, apoptosis, senescence, metastasis) vs. the bioelectric/morphogenetic view of cancer: stem and tumor cells are persistently depolarized while quiescent differentiated cells are hyperpolarized; closing gap junctions electrically isolates nascent tumor cells from tissue-level morphogenetic normalization cues (reversion to unicellular 'atavistic' behavior), and later GJ re-coupling enables invasive 'browbeating' of host neighbors.
equations: V_mem,differentiated (-70 to -90 mV) << V_mem,stem/tumor (-10 to -30 mV)
Tumor initiation: G_GJ -> 0 (electrical isolation from tissue homeostasis)
nodes.DiagnosticQuestion: How does the bioelectric model explain tumor induction without DNA mutations (and tumor suppression despite oncogenic mutations) via V_mem depolarization and gap-junctional isolation?
